questions.question: A developer has corrected Claude three times about the same misunderstanding, and its answers keep drifting back. The session is long and full of discarded attempts. What is the best move?
options: Keep correcting, using stronger wording and more capital letters each time the mistake reappears
Compact the conversation and continue, since the summary will keep only what is useful
Clear the session and start again with a more specific prompt that includes what was learned
Switch to a different permission mode so that Claude pays closer attention to the corrections
questions.explanation: After repeated failed corrections the context is cluttered with wrong approaches, and a fresh session with a sharper prompt usually outperforms patching. Compaction would carry the clutter forward in summary form, emphasis does not fix a misunderstanding, and permission modes do not affect attention.

questions.question: Claude reported that a new CSV importer was finished, but it breaks on fields that contain quoted commas. Which change best prevents this in future tasks?
options: Ask Claude to review its own work carefully before it says that it is done
Tell Claude to be more careful about edge cases at the start of every prompt
Read every diff by hand before accepting any change from Claude
Provide runnable verification, such as tests with representative inputs including quoted fields, and have Claude run them until they pass
questions.explanation: A check Claude can run closes the loop, so it keeps working until the evidence says the job is right. Asking for care or self-review relies on the same judgment that missed the case, and reading every diff by hand does not scale and leaves you as the verification loop.

questions.question: A team wants Claude to implement a rate limiter with specific burst and refill behavior. Which workflow most reliably produces a correct implementation?
options: Write tests for the expected behavior, edge cases and performance first, then have Claude implement and iterate on the failures
Have Claude write both the limiter and its tests in a single pass, then trust the passing result
Describe the burst and refill behavior in detail and verify the implementation by reading the code
Ask Claude to implement the limiter now and add tests only after users report problems
questions.explanation: Tests written first define the target independently of the implementation, and sharing failures steers each iteration. Letting Claude write both in one pass can encode the same misunderstanding in code and tests, reading code is a weaker check than running it, and adding tests after complaints comes too late.

questions.question: Which two actions fit test-driven iteration with Claude Code? (Choose two.)
options: Ask Claude to delete tests it considers redundant before it starts
Disable a failing test temporarily so that Claude can finish the feature
Write tests that cover expected behavior and edge cases before the implementation exists
Describe failures in general terms to avoid anchoring Claude on one case
Paste the failing test output back to Claude after each attempt
questions.explanation: Tests first and failures shared back are the two halves of the loop: a target, then concrete feedback. Disabling tests, vague failure descriptions and letting Claude prune tests all weaken the signal the loop depends on.

questions.question: When several bugs interact, describing them together in one detailed message is generally better than fixing them one at a time.
questions.explanation: Fixes to interacting problems can invalidate each other, so Claude needs the whole picture. Independent problems, by contrast, can be handled one after another.

questions.question: In the interview pattern, the developer must write a complete specification before Claude is allowed to ask any questions.
questions.explanation: The pattern is the reverse: Claude asks questions first to surface considerations the developer may have missed, and the answers become the spec.

questions.question: A CI step posts Claude's review as inline pull-request comments by parsing the prose with regular expressions, and it breaks whenever the wording changes. What is the best fix?
options: Tell Claude to always write findings in one fixed sentence template and keep the regular expressions
Run in print mode with JSON output and a schema for the findings, then read the structured_output field
Switch to streaming output and parse the individual tokens as they arrive from the model
Run the review twice and post only those findings whose wording matches in both runs
questions.explanation: A schema-constrained result gives the pipeline machine-readable fields such as file, line and severity, so wording no longer matters. A template is still free text, token-level parsing is even more fragile, and comparing wording across two runs only discards findings.

questions.question: In a pipeline, the same Claude session that wrote a feature is then asked to review it before merge. Its reviews rarely find anything. What is the best change?
options: Tell the same session to take a more critical stance and to look harder for problems
Ask the same session to think for longer before it approves its own change
Run the review in a separate, fresh invocation that sees only the diff and the criteria
Run the same session's review twice and require both runs to find the same issues
questions.explanation: A session that wrote the code still holds its own reasoning and tends to defend its decisions, whereas an independent instance questions them. Instructions to be critical, extra thinking time and repeated self-review do not remove that bias.

questions.question: After every new commit to a pull request, the review job posts the same nine comments again plus one new one, and developers have started to ignore the bot. What is the best change?
options: Delete all of the bot's earlier comments before each run and then post the complete list again
Run the review only when the pull request is merged instead of on each commit
Ask Claude to shorten each comment so that the repeated ones take up less space
Include the earlier findings in the prompt and tell Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues
questions.explanation: The model does not remember the previous run, so the pipeline must supply the earlier findings and ask for only what is new or unresolved. Deleting and reposting still repeats everything, moving the review to merge time loses the feedback loop, and shorter comments leave the duplication in place.

questions.question: A CI job that generates test suggestions keeps proposing scenarios the suite already covers. What is the best fix?
options: Provide the existing test files in the context and tell Claude to avoid scenarios they already cover
Ask for fewer suggestions per run so that the duplicates are less noticeable to reviewers
Run the job less often so that developers see fewer repeated suggestions over the month
Cap the number of turns for each run so that Claude stops earlier and proposes less
questions.explanation: Claude cannot avoid duplicates it cannot see, so the existing tests must be in context. Asking for fewer suggestions, running less often or capping turns only hides the symptom.

questions.question: Tests generated in CI are trivial, such as getters and framework behavior, and they ignore the project's fixtures. The job runs claude -p inside the repository. Which change is most effective?
options: Add the phrase "write high-quality tests" to the end of every CI prompt
Document the testing standards, what makes a test worth writing, and the available fixtures in the project's instruction file
Generate three times as many tests and discard those that do not increase coverage
Move the job to the Message Batches API so that the model has more time to think per test
questions.explanation: The instruction file is how project context reaches a non-interactive run, so recording the standards, the criteria for valuable tests and the fixtures steers generation. A generic quality request adds no information, filtering by coverage keeps trivial tests that still raise coverage, and batch processing changes cost and latency, not guidance.

questions.question: A nightly job on a shared runner that holds production credentials runs claude -p to fix lint errors, and it sometimes stalls on a permission prompt. What is the best configuration?
options: Run with bypassPermissions so that nothing can ever prompt, since the job is unattended anyway
Pipe the word "yes" into the job's standard input so that every prompt is accepted
Pre-approve the exact tools needed with --allowedTools and use dontAsk mode so that anything else is denied
Add "do not ask for permission" to the prompt text so that Claude proceeds without waiting
questions.explanation: dontAsk turns every unapproved action into a denial instead of a wait, and the allowed list covers what the task needs. Bypassing all checks on a runner with production credentials is unsafe, because that mode is meant for isolated environments; piped input does not reliably answer permission dialogs; and prompt text cannot switch permission behavior off.

questions.question: A team wants Claude to review every pull request automatically when it is opened, without anyone mentioning @claude. How should the GitHub Action step be configured?
options: Leave the prompt empty, because the action reviews every pull request on its own once it is installed
Ask developers to comment @claude on each pull request so that the action wakes up and starts
Raise the maximum number of turns so that the action keeps listening for newly opened pull requests
Give the action a prompt input that describes the review, and trigger the workflow on pull-request events
questions.explanation: With a prompt input the action runs in automation mode on whatever event triggers the workflow. Without a prompt it waits for the trigger phrase, so an empty prompt reviews nothing, relying on manual mentions defeats the automation, and a turn limit has nothing to do with triggering.

questions.question: Reviews in CI began ignoring the project's conventions after the team added --bare to the claude -p command for reproducibility. What explains this, and what is the fix?
options: Bare mode skips automatic loading of instruction files, so the guidance must be passed explicitly, for example with --append-system-prompt-file
Print mode never reads instruction files, so the conventions must be moved into the settings file instead
Bare mode disables the model's ability to follow instructions, so the flag should be removed permanently
Instruction files are read only from the home directory in CI, so they must be copied there first
questions.explanation: Bare mode skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and instruction files so that runs are reproducible, and context must then be supplied through flags such as an appended system prompt file. Without bare mode, print mode loads the project's instruction file as usual.

questions.question: A team's committed .claude/settings.json sets the default model for the repository. One developer prefers a different model in this repository only and does not want to commit a change. Where should she put the override?
options: In ~/.claude/settings.json, because user settings always override project settings
In .claude/settings.local.json, which ranks above the shared project file and stays out of version control
In the committed .claude/settings.json, then ask teammates to override it back if they disagree
In CLAUDE.local.md, since it is also a personal file that sits next to the project settings
questions.explanation: The project-local settings file sits above the shared project file in precedence and is kept out of git, so only her sessions change. User settings rank below project settings, editing the committed file changes it for everyone, and a CLAUDE.local.md file holds instructions for Claude, not settings.

questions.question: A project's settings contain a deny rule for Bash(aws *) and, from another file, an allow rule for Bash(aws s3 ls). What happens when Claude tries to run aws s3 ls?
options: The call runs, because the narrower allow rule is more specific than the broad deny
The call runs only if the user's settings file sets the allow rule, since user rules outrank project rules
The call is blocked, because deny rules are evaluated before allow rules and the first match decides
Claude Code asks for confirmation each time, because the two rules cancel each other out
questions.explanation: Rules are checked in the order deny, ask, allow, and the first match wins, so a broad deny cannot be carved out by a narrower allow. Specificity does not change the order, file origin does not make an allow outrank a deny, and the rules do not cancel.

questions.question: Which two practices help CI-invoked Claude Code generate useful tests? (Choose two.)
options: Ask for the largest possible number of tests to maximize coverage
Let the job pause for interactive approval before each test file is written
Document the project's testing standards and available fixtures where the run can read them
Provide the existing test files so that suggestions avoid scenarios already covered
Strip out all project context so that every run starts from an identical blank state
questions.explanation: Seeing what already exists and knowing the conventions are what make suggestions new and fitting. Maximizing quantity produces low-value tests, interactive pauses stall an unattended job, and removing context removes exactly the information needed.

questions.question: Which two statements about running Claude Code in a pipeline are correct? (Choose two.)
options: The --ci flag switches Claude Code to the Message Batches API at half price
When no terminal is attached, permission prompts are answered automatically with the safest option
Setting CLAUDE_NONINTERACTIVE=1 is the documented way to avoid hangs
With --output-format json and --json-schema, the structured result is returned in the structured_output field
The -p flag runs a single prompt non-interactively, prints the result and exits
questions.explanation: Print mode and the structured-output flags are documented, parseable pipeline features. The other three describe things that do not exist or that Claude Code does not do: there is no such flag or variable, and permission requests nobody can answer are denied, or must be pre-approved, rather than auto-answered.

questions.question: A session that generated code is just as effective at reviewing its own changes as a fresh, independent Claude instance.
questions.explanation: The generating session retains its own reasoning and is less likely to question its decisions. An independent instance reviewing only the diff and criteria catches subtler issues.

questions.question: When a review is rerun after new commits, including the earlier findings in the prompt and asking for only new or unresolved issues reduces duplicate comments.
questions.explanation: The model does not remember the previous run, so the pipeline has to supply the earlier findings.

questions.question: Running Claude Code with --bare skips automatic loading of CLAUDE.md, so project guidance must then be supplied another way.
questions.explanation: Bare mode skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and instruction files. Pass what you need with flags such as an appended system prompt file.

lessons.title: The Agentic Loop and Task Decomposition
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 1.1 and 1.6: how an agent loop runs on stop_reason, how tool results reach the next step, which termination shortcuts fail, and when to use a prompt chain versus adaptive decomposition.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 1.1 (agentic loops) and 1.6 (task decomposition). An agent is a loop wrapped around a model. You give Claude a goal, a list of tools and the conversation so far. It answers either with a final reply or with a request: run this tool with these arguments. Claude never runs your tools itself. Your code, or the Claude Agent SDK, which ships the loop ready-made, runs the tool, adds the output to the conversation and asks again. That repeat-until-done cycle is the agentic loop.

The control flow hangs on one field of every API response, stop_reason. When it is "tool_use", the response contains one or more tool_use blocks, each with an id, a tool name and an input object. You execute them and send a new user message holding one tool_result block per request, matched by id and placed before any text. When it is "end_turn", Claude is finished and the loop exits. "max_tokens" means the reply was cut off; if it ends in a half-written tool request, retry with a larger limit instead of running the fragment. The Messages API is stateless, so every request carries the whole history: the assistant message with its tool requests and the user message with the results. That appended history is how Claude "remembers" what a tool returned. If one response asks for several independent tools, return all results together; read-only calls may run concurrently.

This design is model-driven: Claude reads the latest results and decides what to call next, or whether to stop. The alternative is a pre-configured decision tree, where your code fixes the order of tools. Trees are predictable and fine when the steps really are known, but they cannot react to what a result reveals. The exam expects you to spot three anti-patterns for ending a loop. Scanning Claude's prose for "all done" breaks when the wording changes. Treating the existence of text as completion fails because Claude often writes a sentence beside a tool request. Making an iteration cap the primary stop cuts off tasks that need more steps. Caps still belong as a safety net: the Agent SDK's maxTurns and budget limits end a run with an error result (error_max_turns, error_max_budget_usd), so check the subtype before reading the text; only success carries a final answer.

Task statement 1.6 asks how to break big work into steps. A prompt chain is a fixed sequence of focused calls: extract, then validate, then summarize. Use it when the steps are predictable and repeat on every input. For code review the standard chain is a per-file pass for local problems, then a separate integration pass on data flow across files. The reason is attention dilution: when a model reviews many files at once, depth becomes uneven, bugs slip through and the same pattern gets contradictory verdicts. A bigger context window does not cure that; narrower passes do.

Open-ended work needs the opposite, dynamic and adaptive decomposition. To add tests to a legacy billing system nobody understands, a checklist written before looking at the code is wrong within the hour. Map the structure first, find the high-impact or risky areas, write a prioritized plan, and revise it whenever a new dependency appears. Predictable steps call for a chain; unpredictable discoveries call for a plan that adapts.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to agentic loops? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of a contractor who has no hands of her own and works through an assistant on the phone. She says "measure the kitchen window", the assistant does it and reports back, and she decides what to ask next. She hangs up only when she says "that is everything I need". A fixed checklist would be a script the assistant follows whatever the measurements show. The loop is the phone call, and the closing sentence is the signal that ends it; listening to the assistant's chatter for hints that she must be finished would be the mistake.
commonTraps: Ending the loop because a reply contains text, or because it says "done", is wrong; the stop reason decides.
A turn or iteration cap is a safety net that ends the run with an error result, not the normal way an agent finishes.
The API is stateless, so leaving out the assistant's tool requests or the matching results makes the agent lose its place.
A bigger context window does not fix inconsistent multi-file reviews; focused per-file passes plus an integration pass do.
lessons.scenario: A team builds a returns assistant on the Messages API. Their first loop stopped whenever a response contained text and often quit mid-task. They now continue while the stop reason is tool_use, finish on end_turn, resend the full history each time, and keep a maximum-turns guardrail that returns a clear error. For a weekly audit of return policies they use a fixed chain of extract, validate and summarize, while for investigating odd refund patterns they let the agent plan adaptively.
lessons.onTheJob: Log the stop reason of every response and the number of loop iterations per task; a sudden change in either is the earliest warning that a prompt or tool change broke something. Keep guardrails such as a turn limit, a spending cap and timeouts, but make each produce a specific, handled outcome so a capped run can be resumed rather than silently going wrong. Reach for a fixed chain first when the work is predictable: it is cheaper, easier to test and easier to explain than an agent. Add adaptivity only where discoveries really change the plan.

lessons.title: Coordinators, Subagents and Context Passing
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 1.2 and 1.3: hub-and-spoke orchestration, subagent definitions and isolation, explicit context passing, parallel spawning, and the coordinator's decomposition, selection and refinement duties.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 1.2 and 1.3. A single agent has one context window and one toolbox. When a job is broad, such as a cited research report, you split it across specialists: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes, one writes the report. The common shape is hub-and-spoke. A coordinator agent receives the request, decomposes it, delegates to subagents, collects what they return and decides what happens next. Subagents never talk to each other; everything passes through the coordinator, which gives you one place to log, one place to handle errors consistently and one place to control what each agent sees.

A subagent is a separate agent instance with its own context window, system prompt and tool list. In the Agent SDK you describe each type with an AgentDefinition (a description that tells the coordinator when to use it, a system prompt, and the tools it may use) and the coordinator starts instances by calling the subagent-launching tool. The exam guide calls that tool Task and expects the coordinator's allowed tools to include it; current SDK documentation calls it Agent and still accepts the old name. The key fact is isolation. A subagent does not inherit the coordinator's conversation, earlier tool results or other subagents' work. The only channel from parent to child is the prompt string, and the only channel back is the child's final message. A delegation prompt must therefore be self-contained: the goal, the quality bar, the actual findings to build on, the output format and any constraints. "Summarize what the search agent found" fails if those findings were never pasted in.

Pass structured records rather than prose. If each finding carries the claim, an evidence excerpt, the source URL or document name, the page and the date, attribution survives every hand-off, whereas a flowing paragraph is where citations die. Write coordinator prompts as goals and quality criteria rather than rigid step lists, so a subagent can adapt when a site is blocked or a source is empty.

The coordinator earns its keep in four jobs. It decomposes: if it splits "the future of urban transport" into three subtasks that all concern e-scooters, every subagent can succeed and the report still ignores buses, rail and cycling. When a report has gaps and the subagents look healthy, read the coordinator's subtask list first. It selects: a quick factual lookup should not trigger the full pipeline. It partitions scope, by subtopic, region or source type, so parallel agents do not duplicate each other. And it refines: after synthesis it checks for gaps, sends targeted queries to the search and analysis agents, and re-runs synthesis until coverage is adequate.

Speed comes from parallelism. If the coordinator needs four independent lookups, it should emit four launch calls in a single response; they run concurrently and the total time approaches the slowest one. Launched over four turns, the time is the sum. At the session level, a fork copies a session's history into an independent branch so two approaches can start from the same analysis. Two anti-patterns recur: shared mutable state between subagents, such as a common scratchpad both write to, and peer-to-peer messaging that bypasses the hub.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to multi-agent systems? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Picture a newsroom editor running a story on regional flooding. She does not write everything herself: she sends one reporter to the council records, one to interview engineers, and one to check insurance data. Each reporter works alone and can only use the notes on the assignment sheet she hands over, because none of them sat in her planning meeting. When they return, the editor reads their notes, notices that nobody covered funding, sends someone back with a precise question, and only then lets the writer draft the piece.
commonTraps: Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's history; a short prompt such as "use the earlier results" leaves them blind.
Gaps in a report whose subagents all succeeded usually mean the coordinator's decomposition was too narrow.
Parallelism needs several launch calls in one response; one call per turn is sequential.
Shared scratchpads and agent-to-agent messaging bypass the hub and hide failures.
lessons.scenario: A policy research firm asks its coordinator how small cities are preparing for extreme heat. The coordinator picks three partitions (cooling infrastructure, public health programs, funding sources) and launches the three search subagents in one response. It passes each the goal, scope and a required record format with source URL and date. The first synthesis lacks anything on funding, so the coordinator sends one targeted follow-up query and re-runs synthesis before the report agent is invoked.
lessons.onTheJob: Read the coordinator's decomposition before you read anything else when output quality drops; most coverage bugs are visible there. Write delegation prompts as if the subagent were a smart contractor who has never seen the project: objective, boundaries, the material, the output format, and what to do when data is missing. Keep a subagent's final report short and structured, because that message is all the coordinator receives. Limit each specialist to the tools of its role, and log every launch and return at the hub so you can replay a run.

lessons.title: Enforcement, Hooks and Human Handoffs
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 1.4 and 1.5: prompt guidance versus programmatic enforcement, prerequisite gates, pre- and post-execution hooks, result normalization, structured handoffs and multi-concern requests.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 1.4 and 1.5. Some rules are style: be concise, apologize for delays. If the model occasionally forgets, little is lost. Other rules are obligations: verify the customer before touching money, never approve a payment above a limit, never send privileged documents to an outside service. For these the exam draws a hard line. Prompt instructions, however emphatic, and few-shot examples are probabilistic. The model follows them almost always, which still means sometimes not. Where one miss costs money or exposes data, enforce the rule in code.

Two code-level tools carry most of the weight. A prerequisite gate sits in the layer that executes tools. When the model asks for process_refund before get_customer has returned a verified customer id, the gate refuses and returns an error saying what to do first; the model then calls the verification tool. Hooks are callbacks the Agent SDK runs at fixed points in the loop. A PreToolUse hook runs before a tool executes and can allow, deny, ask about or rewrite the call (the decision field is permissionDecision, and rewriting arguments uses updatedInput). A deny blocks the call and its reason is returned to the model, so write the reason as a redirect: "refund exceeds the limit; escalate to a human with a case summary". When several hooks answer differently the strictest wins, so deny beats defer, ask and allow. A PostToolUse hook runs after the tool returns and can add context or replace the result before the model reads it.

Two details trip people up. First, a hook's matcher selects by tool name, such as Bash, Write|Edit, or a pattern for every tool of one MCP server, never by arguments. To act on an amount or a file path, read the tool input inside the callback. Second, timing: prevention and argument rewriting belong before execution, while normalization and enrichment belong after. A post-execution hook cannot undo a payment. Hooks run in your application process, so they use no context tokens and the model cannot argue its way past them.

Normalization is the classic post-execution job. Suppose three MCP tools return a date as a Unix timestamp, an ISO 8601 string and a numeric status code. Rather than explaining every format in the prompt, convert them in a post-execution hook so that the model only ever sees one convention.

Humans enter through escalation. A human agent often cannot see the AI conversation, so the handoff must stand alone: customer id, root cause, amounts, actions already taken and a recommended next step. Make the escalation tool's input schema require those fields so a thin handoff cannot be produced. And when a customer message holds several problems, split it into distinct items, investigate them in parallel using the same verified customer context, and reply once with a unified resolution.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to enforcement and hooks? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A bank teller is trained to check ID before any withdrawal. That is guidance. The vault door that will not open until a manager turns a key is enforcement. A good bank uses both: training for judgment, the door for the rule that must never be broken. When the door refuses, a note on it says "needs manager approval, ring the bell", so the teller knows the next step. A pre-execution hook is that door, and its denial reason is the note.
commonTraps: Few-shot examples and stronger wording never provide a guarantee; if the stem mentions money or security, choose the code-level control.
Pre-execution hooks prevent and rewrite; post-execution hooks transform results. A post-execution hook cannot stop a payment.
Matchers match tool names, not arguments; the argument check happens inside the callback.
A denial without a reason strands the agent, so point to the alternative workflow in the message.
A raw transcript or a vague note is a weaker handoff than a structured summary.
lessons.scenario: A telecom billing agent has lookup_account, apply_credit and escalate_to_human tools. The team adds a gate so apply_credit is rejected until lookup_account has returned a verified account id, and a pre-execution hook that denies credits above $200 with the message "above limit; escalate with case summary". A post-execution hook converts the three date formats returned by legacy systems. The escalate tool requires account id, root cause, amount, actions taken and recommended action.
lessons.onTheJob: Start by listing which rules are obligations and which are preferences; only the first group needs hooks and gates, and over-engineering the second group adds maintenance for no benefit. Write every denial message for the model: what was blocked, why, and what to do instead. Test enforcement by trying to break it, for example by asking for a refund before identifying yourself. Keep a log of denials; a rising count shows where the prompt and the policy disagree. Treat hook callbacks like production code, with timeouts and error handling, since a failing hook can block real work.

lessons.title: Sessions: Resume, Fork or Start Fresh
lessons.summary: Covers task statement 1.7: named sessions and resumption, fork_session for divergent approaches, and choosing between resuming with a change note and starting fresh with an injected summary.
lessons.reading:
Task statement 1.7 is about continuity. A session is the saved conversation of an agent run: your prompts, every tool call, every result and every reply. Claude Code and the Agent SDK write it to disk so you can return later with the context intact. Two facts matter more than the mechanics. First, a session stores the conversation, not your files: it remembers what the agent read, not whether the file has changed since. Second, you must choose on purpose between three ways forward: resume, fork, or start fresh.

Resuming continues an existing session with its whole history. In Claude Code you name a session (claude -n auth-refactor at startup, or /rename inside the session) and later reopen it with claude --resume auth-refactor, while claude --continue reopens the most recent session in the directory. In the SDK you capture the session id from the final result message and pass it as resume, and the continue option picks the most recent one automatically. Use the targeted form whenever several sessions exist, for example one per customer or one per investigation. Resuming the same session in two terminals without forking interleaves both conversations into one transcript, so do not.

Forking starts a new session as a copy of an existing one: the fork_session option in the SDK, or --fork-session and /branch in Claude Code. The copy gets its own id and the original stays as it was. This is how you explore divergent approaches from a shared analysis baseline. Spend an hour mapping a payment module once, then fork twice to compare two testing strategies or two refactorings. Remember what a fork does not branch: files. If both branches edit code in the same directory, the edits collide, so give edit-heavy experiments separate worktrees or copies.

The hard judgment is staleness. A resumed session still holds the outputs of old Read and Bash calls. If a teammate rewrote four files overnight, the agent may reason confidently from contents that no longer exist. You have two good options. When most earlier work is still valid, resume and tell the agent exactly which files changed, so it re-reads those instead of repeating the whole exploration. When many things changed, or the history is long and mostly obsolete, start a new session and inject a structured summary of the findings you still trust. The SDK documentation makes a similar point about moving sessions between machines: capturing results as state and passing them into a fresh prompt is often more robust than shipping transcripts around.

A rule of thumb ties it together. Mostly valid context: resume, plus a note about what changed. Mostly stale context: start fresh with a summary. Several alternatives to try from the same understanding: fork.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to sessions? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A resumed session is like returning to a half-finished jigsaw puzzle on the dining table. Your earlier progress is all there, but someone may have moved pieces while you were away. Forking is photocopying your progress notes so two people can try different strategies; the pieces on the table are still shared, so anything that moves pieces needs a second table. Starting fresh with a summary is sitting down at a clean table with a note that says "the border and the sky are done".
commonTraps: Sessions store conversations, not files, so a resumed or forked agent does not know that files changed unless it is told.
The continue option reopens the most recent session, which may not be the one you want; use resume with a name or id.
Resuming the same session in two places mixes the histories; fork to branch.
Trusting a long, mostly outdated history is riskier than starting fresh from a short summary.
lessons.scenario: An engineer names a session "billing-test-plan" and maps the billing module over two days. A teammate then refactors five files. She resumes the session, lists the five changed files, and the agent re-reads only those before proposing tests. Later she forks the session twice to compare a contract-test strategy with a snapshot-test strategy, each in its own git worktree. After a quarter-end merge touches most modules, she begins a new session seeded with a one-page summary of the findings that survived.
lessons.onTheJob: Name sessions the moment you start anything that may span days, and put the task in the name. Before resuming, check what changed in version control since the session was last active and decide whether a change note will do or a restart is cleaner. Keep a short findings file or summary as you work; it doubles as the seed for a fresh session and as protection against context loss. Fork only when you genuinely want to compare alternatives, and give each branch its own worktree if it will write code.

lessons.title: Tool Descriptions, Error Responses and Tool Distribution
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3: writing descriptions that separate similar tools, structured MCP error responses, scoping tools to roles, and what tool_choice guarantees.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3. When Claude chooses a tool it consults only what you show it: the tool's name, its description and its input schema. It never sees your code, so the description does the selecting. A line such as "Retrieves customer information" beside "Retrieves order details" produces unreliable picks when both take similar identifiers. A strong description says what the tool does, which inputs it accepts with an example format, what it returns, the edge cases, and the boundary: when to use it instead of a similar tool.

Overlap is the enemy. If analyze_content and analyze_document read almost the same, rename and rewrite them so each has a distinct purpose, for example one built for extracting web results. A generic tool that extracts, summarizes and fact-checks, with a different output shape for each, should be split into purpose-specific tools with defined input and output contracts. (The documentation also advises grouping closely related operations; the shared principle is that every tool has one clear purpose.) Then read the system prompt: "always check billing history for billing questions" can wire a keyword to a tool and override good descriptions.

Errors are the other half of the contract. In MCP a failed call comes back inside a normal result with isError set to true, so the model sees the failure as data it can act on; faults in the request itself, like an unknown tool, are JSON-RPC errors. Inside the result, a useful convention, which the exam calls structured error metadata, is a category, an isRetryable flag and a readable message (the field names are yours; the protocol defines only isError). Transient errors such as timeouts deserve a retry. Validation errors need a corrected input. Business errors, such as a refund outside the window, are final: mark them not retryable and include wording the agent can pass to the customer. Permission errors need other access or a human. A uniform "Operation failed" hides all of this, and an empty result returned for an outage is worse: zero matches is a valid answer, a timeout is not.

Where tools live matters as much as how they are written. Give one agent eighteen tools and its selection degrades; give a specialist the four or five its role needs. Out-of-role tools get misused, like web search in a synthesis agent. When a specialist has a frequent, simple need, add one narrow tool (a verify_fact lookup for the synthesis agent) and route rare heavy cases through the coordinator. Swap risky generic tools for constrained ones, such as a validating load_document instead of fetch-any-URL.

Finally, tool_choice. "auto" lets the model answer in text or call tools. "any" requires some tool call and lets the model choose which, which suits several extraction tools when the document type is unknown. Naming a tool forces that call, which suits "run extract_metadata first", with later turns back on auto. Forcing prefills the reply, so no explanation comes before the call. Not every model or setting accepts the forced modes: manual extended thinking rejects them, and current documentation lists newer models where the substitute is automatic choice with strict tool use, which makes inputs match your schema (valid shape, not necessarily sensible values).
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to tool design? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: A tool description is the label on a drawer in a workshop. A label reading "Tools" tells an apprentice nothing, but "Phillips screwdrivers, sizes 0 to 3, for electronics; for wood screws use the next drawer" lets a newcomer pick correctly without asking. If two drawers carry nearly the same label, even a skilled apprentice guesses. It also helps to hand the apprentice only the drawers needed for today's job instead of the entire warehouse.
commonTraps: Few-shot examples or a routing layer are not the first fix for confusion between similar tools; fix the descriptions and names first.
A business-rule failure is not retryable, and retrying it only wastes calls.
An outage reported as "no results" is silent error suppression, whereas a genuine empty result is a success.
tool_choice auto can return plain text; only requiring a tool (any, or a named tool) guarantees a call, and both skip the explanatory preamble.
More tools for one agent is not more capability: past a handful, selection reliability falls.
lessons.scenario: A logistics assistant has track_shipment and lookup_order, each with a one-line description, and it sends tracking numbers to the wrong one. The team rewrites both descriptions with accepted formats, example queries and an explicit boundary. The refund tool now returns a business error flagged non-retryable, with a customer-friendly sentence, once the window has passed, and a retryable transient error for timeouts. In the research agents, the synthesis agent keeps only a narrow verify_fact tool instead of web search.
lessons.onTheJob: Write tool descriptions the way you would brief a new colleague: what the tool is for, what it is not for, what goes in, what comes out, and one example. Test selection with ambiguous requests such as "check on my order" and read the transcripts; wrong picks usually trace to a thin description or a keyword-heavy line in the system prompt. Standardize one error payload across every tool you own so the agent learns a single vocabulary of failures. When an agent needs a new capability, ask whether another specialist should own it before widening anyone's toolbox.

lessons.title: MCP Servers, Scopes and the Built-in Tools
lessons.summary: Covers task statements 2.4 and 2.5: MCP tools, resources and prompts, project versus user scope, environment variable expansion, descriptions that compete with built-ins, and choosing between Grep, Glob, Read, Write and Edit.
lessons.reading:
This lesson covers task statements 2.4 and 2.5. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to outside systems. A host application creates one client per server, and each server can offer three kinds of capability. Tools are actions the model chooses to invoke. Resources are read-only content addressed by URI, such as documentation pages, database schemas or issue summaries, that the application decides how to surface. Prompts are templates the user selects, usually as slash commands. Servers cannot see the whole conversation or each other, and in the current specification (dated 2026-07-28) every request is self-contained.

Configuration is mostly a question of scope. A project-scoped server lives in .mcp.json at the repository root and is committed, so every teammate gets the same tooling (Claude Code asks for approval first). A user-scoped server lives in your own ~/.claude.json and follows you across projects without touching anyone else, which suits personal or experimental servers. Claude Code also has a local scope, the default for claude mcp add: private to you, tied to the current project, and again stored in ~/.claude.json. If one name is defined in several places, the highest-precedence entry wins whole (local, then project, then user). All configured servers connect together, so a shared GitHub server and your experimental one are usable in the same session. Keep secrets out of the file with environment variable expansion, such as "Authorization": "Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN}" or ${VAR:-default}, and each person supplies the variable.

Claude Code defers MCP tool definitions by default: only names load at the start and full definitions are fetched on demand. MCP tools appear as mcp__server__tool, which is also how permission rules and hook matchers refer to them. Write rich MCP tool descriptions: if the agent keeps using the built-in text search instead of your symbol-aware search tool, the description is probably too thin to compete. And expose catalogs as resources: if the agent wastes calls discovering what exists, publish the documentation hierarchy or schema list as a resource. Prefer an existing community server for a standard integration such as Jira, and reserve custom servers for team-specific workflows.

The built-in tools are the other half. Grep searches file contents (callers of a function, an error message, an import). Glob matches file paths (every **/*.test.tsx). Read loads a whole file. Write creates a file or overwrites it with the full content you supply. Edit replaces exact text, which must appear exactly once; if it matches in several places the edit fails, and you either add surrounding lines to make the anchor unique or fall back to reading the file and writing the updated whole. (In some Claude Code setups search runs through the shell; the roles stay the same.)

Do not read all 3,000 files of an unfamiliar service. Search for the entry point (a refund route, an error string), read the file it points to, and follow its imports with more searches. When a function is re-exported through wrapper modules under other names, first list each wrapper's exported names and then search for every one of them; searching only the original name misses the real callers.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to MCP? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: MCP is like a standard wall socket for tools. The host is the building, each server is an appliance plugged into its own socket, and the shared plug shape is the protocol, so any appliance fits. The project-level .mcp.json is the building plan listing the sockets every office has, while your user-level file is the desk lamp you brought from home. The built-in tools are the instruments in your pocket: a magnifying glass for text inside documents (Grep), a directory board for names on doors (Glob), and a pencil for exact corrections (Edit).
commonTraps: Committing a token in .mcp.json is wrong; reference ${VAR} and rotate any secret that leaked.
Project scope is shared through version control and user scope is private, yet tools from all configured servers are available together.
An agent preferring a built-in tool over your MCP tool is a description problem, not a reason to disable the built-in.
Glob finds file names, Grep finds text inside files, and mixing them up is a frequent wrong answer.
A failed targeted edit is fixed with a unique anchor or a read-then-write, not by repeating the edit or using replace-all blindly.
lessons.scenario: A team commits a project .mcp.json that defines a Jira server using ${JIRA_TOKEN}, while one developer keeps an experimental code-search server in her user config. The team also publishes the documentation hierarchy as an MCP resource so agents stop spending calls listing pages. Asked how refunds flow through an unfamiliar service, the agent searches for the refund route, reads the handler and follows the imports; later it finds a wrapper that re-exports a helper under a new name and searches for each exported name.
lessons.onTheJob: Treat .mcp.json like any committed configuration: review it in pull requests, never allow literal credentials, and document which variables a newcomer must set. Put experiments at user scope and promote them to the project file only when the team agrees. Watch transcripts for the agent ignoring a server, which almost always means the description undersells the tool. Teach newcomers the exploration habit of search first and read second, and keep an eye on output size, since huge tool results eat context quickly.

cheatSheet.heading: Agentic loop and task decomposition (1.1, 1.6)
points: Loop: send history and tools, then read stop_reason. "tool_use" means run every requested tool, append the assistant message and ONE user message holding a tool_result per id (results first, text after), and call again. "end_turn" means finished.
max_tokens with a half-written tool request: retry with a larger limit and never run the fragment. The Messages API is stateless, so the full history is resent on every call.

Termination anti-patterns: parsing prose for "done", treating any text as completion, and using an iteration cap as the primary stop. Caps (maxTurns, budget) are guardrails that end in error_max_turns or error_max_budget_usd; only subtype success carries a result.
Model-driven decisions adapt to tool results; pre-configured decision trees and fixed tool sequences are predictable but cannot adapt.
Parallel tool calls: return all tool_result blocks together in one user message. Read-only tools may run concurrently; Edit, Write and Bash run one at a time.

Prompt chaining = fixed, sequential steps for predictable multi-aspect work. For big reviews use a per-file local pass plus a cross-file integration pass; a larger context window does not cure attention dilution.
Dynamic decomposition for open-ended work: map the structure, find high-impact areas, build a prioritized plan, and revise it as dependencies surface.

cheatSheet.heading: Multi-agent orchestration (1.2, 1.3)
points: Hub-and-spoke: the coordinator decomposes, selects subagents by query complexity, delegates, aggregates, and judges coverage. ALL communication goes through it. No peer-to-peer messaging and no shared mutable scratchpad.
Subagents have isolated context: no parent history, no earlier tool results, no memory between invocations. The prompt is the only channel in; the final message is the only channel out.

The spawning tool is Task in the exam guide; current SDK and Claude Code docs call it Agent and still accept Task. The coordinator must be allowed to use it. An AgentDefinition holds a description, a system prompt and a tool list (optionally a model).
Pass complete findings in the prompt as structured records: claim, evidence, source URL or document, page, date. Keep content separate from metadata so attribution survives.
Parallel subagents = several launch calls in ONE coordinator response. One call per turn is sequential and costs the sum of the durations.
Coordinator prompts state goals and quality criteria, not step-by-step scripts. Partition scope (subtopic, region, source type) to avoid duplication.
Refinement loop: evaluate the synthesis for gaps, send targeted queries to search and analysis, re-run synthesis, and stop on a coverage criterion.
Report has gaps but every subagent succeeded? Read the coordinator's decomposition first.

cheatSheet.heading: Enforcement, hooks, handoffs and sessions (1.4, 1.5, 1.7)
points: Obligations with money, identity or security consequences need programmatic enforcement (prerequisite gates, hooks). Prompts, few-shot examples and capital letters are probabilistic.

PreToolUse hook: allow, deny, ask or defer via permissionDecision; updatedInput rewrites arguments. Deny beats defer, which beats ask, which beats allow. Put the redirect in the denial reason, such as "escalate to a human".
PostToolUse hook: runs after the tool and can add context or replace the result, for example normalizing Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 dates and numeric status codes. It cannot undo a side effect.
Matchers match tool names (Write|Edit, an mcp__server__ prefix), not arguments: inspect the tool input inside the callback. Hooks run outside the context window.
Human handoff when the human cannot see the transcript: customer id, root cause, amounts, actions taken, recommended next step. Make them required fields of the escalation tool.
Multi-concern message: split into distinct items, investigate in parallel with the same verified context, and synthesize one reply.

Sessions store the conversation, not files. claude -n or /rename names a session, claude --resume <name> reopens it, claude --continue reopens the most recent; the SDK uses resume with an id and fork_session to branch.

Mostly valid context: resume and tell the agent which files changed. Mostly stale: start fresh with a structured summary. Alternatives from one baseline: fork (give each branch its own worktree if it edits).

cheatSheet.heading: Tool design, errors and tool_choice (2.1, 2.2, 2.3)
points: Descriptions drive tool selection: purpose, accepted input formats with examples, outputs, edge cases, and a boundary against similar tools. Fix thin or overlapping descriptions and names before adding routers or few-shot examples.

Split overloaded generic tools into purpose-specific ones with clear contracts, and namespace names (github_list_prs). Review the system prompt for keyword-sensitive instructions that override descriptions.

MCP: isError true in the result is a model-visible failure; unknown tools and malformed requests are JSON-RPC protocol errors. Categories: transient (retry), validation (fix the input), business (final, customer-friendly text, not retryable), permission (other access or a human). errorCategory and isRetryable are a convention, not protocol fields.
Never return a uniform "Operation failed" or an empty success for an outage: zero matches is a valid result, a timeout is an access failure.
Subagents retry transient failures locally and propagate only what they cannot fix, with what was attempted and partial results.

Too many tools (18 versus 4-5) degrade selection. Scope tools per role, add a narrow cross-role tool (verify_fact) for frequent small needs, and replace risky generic tools with constrained ones (load_document instead of fetch_url).

tool_choice: auto (default, text possible), any (must call some tool), a named tool (forced), none. Forced and any prefill the reply, so no preamble. They are rejected with manual extended thinking and, per current docs, on several newest models; strict tool use (strict: true) guarantees schema-valid inputs, not sensible values.

cheatSheet.heading: MCP integration and built-in tools (2.4, 2.5)
points: MCP primitives: tools (model-controlled actions), resources (read-only content by URI that the application surfaces; catalogs cut exploratory calls), prompts (user-selected templates).

Scopes: project = .mcp.json, committed and shared; user = ~/.claude.json, private across projects; local (default for claude mcp add) = private to this project, also in ~/.claude.json. Same name in several scopes: the highest-precedence entry wins whole (local, then project, then user).
Secrets: ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} expansion works in command, args, env, url and headers. Never commit tokens; rotate any that leaked.
Tools of all configured servers are available together. Tool search loads names first and fetches definitions on demand. MCP tools are named mcp__server__tool.

Agent prefers Grep over your MCP tool? Enrich the MCP tool description (capabilities, outputs, when to prefer it). Use community servers for standard integrations such as Jira; build custom ones only for team-specific workflows.
Built-ins: Grep = text inside files (callers, errors, imports); Glob = file paths (**/*.test.tsx); Read = whole file; Write = full overwrite; Edit = exact text that must be unique.
Edit fails on non-unique text: add surrounding lines for a unique anchor, or Read then Write. Never repeat the same edit or use replace-all blindly.
Explore incrementally: search for entry points, Read, follow imports. For wrapper modules, list the exported names and search for each one.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: Format: 60 items (multiple choice and multiple response; each item says how many answers to choose) built from 4 scenarios picked at random from a bank of 6. Time limit 120 minutes, so roughly two minutes per item. Proctored online or at a test center.

Scoring: scaled 100 to 1,000 with a pass mark of 720, measured against a fixed standard rather than other candidates. The score report gives percent-correct per domain, but pass or fail depends on the total score only.

Blueprint weights: Agentic Architecture 27%, Tool Design and MCP 18%, Claude Code Configuration 20%, Prompt Engineering and Structured Output 20%, Context Management and Reliability 15%. Domains 1 and 2 together are 45% of the items.

Questions are scenario-based and ask for the BEST or MOST effective approach: one best answer and three plausible but flawed ones. Read the scenario's constraints first (severity of consequences, latency, who can see what).

Reliable principles: code-level enforcement beats prompt guidance when consequences are severe; descriptions are the first fix for tool misrouting; subagents inherit nothing, so pass context explicitly; fix the root cause, using the proportionate first step.

Eliminate options that rely on prompts where a guarantee is needed, that add heavy infrastructure (routers, classifiers) before a simple fix, that blame downstream agents for an upstream decomposition problem, that run independent work sequentially, that share mutable state between agents, or that return generic errors.

For multiple-response items, check the required count first and make sure every choice stands on its own: each correct option should be a complete, defensible answer, and tempting extras usually contain an absolute or an anti-pattern.

Terminology differs between sources: the guide says Task tool, current documentation says Agent tool. Answer by the mechanism. Skip heavy study of out-of-scope topics such as fine-tuning, API billing, hosting MCP servers, computer use, streaming internals and pricing.

If you stall on an item, choose the best remaining answer and move on; a scenario you know well later is worth more than ten extra minutes here. A failed attempt can be retaken after 14 days, then 30, then 90, with up to four attempts in 12 months.

madlibs.scenario: The application keeps calling the model while the stop reason is {b1}, and leaves the loop when the stop reason is {b2}. A counter that ends the loop after a fixed number of rounds is acceptable only as a {b3}, not as the primary stop condition.
