sequences.prompt: Put one pass through the agentic loop in order, from sending the request to presenting the answer.
steps: Send the conversation history and the tool definitions to the model
Read the response and check its stop reason
Execute each tool the model requested
Append the assistant message and a user message with one tool_result per request
Call the model again with the extended history
When the stop reason is end_turn, present the final answer
sequences.explanation: The stop reason decides what happens after each response. Tool results are appended together with the assistant message that requested them, and the whole history goes back to the model. Only an end_turn response is presented as the final answer.

sequences.prompt: Order the coordinator's work in an iterative research run.
steps: Analyze the query and decompose it into distinct subtasks
Launch the chosen subagents in parallel with self-contained prompts
Collect the structured findings and aggregate them
Run synthesis on the aggregated findings
Evaluate the synthesis for coverage gaps
Re-delegate targeted queries for the gaps and re-run synthesis
Deliver the report once coverage is sufficient
sequences.explanation: Decomposition and delegation come first, aggregation and synthesis next, and then the coordinator checks coverage. Gaps trigger targeted re-delegation and another synthesis pass; the loop ends on a coverage criterion.

sequences.prompt: A refund below the approval limit passes through a prerequisite gate, a threshold hook and a normalizing hook. Put the events in order.
steps: The model calls get_customer and receives a verified customer id
The model requests process_refund for an amount below the limit
The gate confirms that a verified customer id exists for the session
The pre-execution hook compares the amount with the approval limit
The refund tool executes
A post-execution hook normalizes the result before the model reads it
sequences.explanation: Identity must be verified before the refund call can pass the gate. The pre-execution checks run before the tool, and only a call that passes both reaches execution. Normalization happens afterwards, on the result, before the model sees it.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps in order for continuing work in a fresh session when an older session's results have become stale.
steps: Review what the old session established and which results are still valid
Write a structured summary of the validated findings
Start a new session
Inject the summary into the new session's first prompt
Tell the agent which areas to verify or re-read
Continue the work from the refreshed baseline
sequences.explanation: The summary is only as good as the review behind it, so validation comes first. The summary is then injected into a clean session, the agent is pointed at the areas that still need checking, and work continues without stale tool results.

sequences.prompt: Order what happens when a search subagent hits a persistent timeout.
steps: The upstream service times out inside the tool
The tool returns a result with the error flag set, a transient category and a retryable marker
The subagent retries locally after a short wait
The retries keep failing
The subagent reports to the coordinator what it attempted and any partial results
The coordinator chooses an alternative source or proceeds with a coverage note
sequences.explanation: Structured error metadata lets the subagent recognize a retryable failure and handle it locally first. Only an error it cannot resolve is propagated, together with the attempts and partial results, so that the coordinator can recover intelligently.

sequences.prompt: Put the steps of exploring an unfamiliar codebase incrementally in order.
steps: Search file contents for an entry point, such as a route or an error string
Read the file the search points to
Follow its imports with targeted searches
List the exported names of any wrapper modules found on the way
Search the codebase for each of those exported names
Summarize the flow from the files actually read
sequences.explanation: Start with a content search instead of reading everything, read only what the trail leads to, and handle re-exports by searching for every exported name rather than only the original one. The summary reflects what was really read.

sequences.prompt: Order the steps for adding a shared MCP server that needs a secret token.
steps: Add the server definition to .mcp.json at the repository root
Reference the token as ${VAR} in the headers or env section
Commit the file to version control
Each teammate sets the variable in their own environment
Approve the project-scoped server the first time Claude Code asks
The agent can now use the server's tools alongside any others
sequences.explanation: The shared file carries only a reference, so it is safe to commit. Each person supplies the secret locally, approves the project server on first use, and then all configured servers are available together.

caseStudies.title: Brightwell Home: A Support Agent Stuck at 61% Resolution
caseStudies.scenario: Brightwell Home sells kitchen appliances online and has built a customer support agent with the Claude Agent SDK. It resolves returns, billing disputes and delivery problems through four custom MCP tools: get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund and escalate_to_human. The target is 80% first-contact resolution; the agent currently reaches 61%. Transcript reviews show four problems. First, get_customer and lookup_order each have a one-line description, and the system prompt says "for any order question, begin by looking up the customer", so pasted order numbers such as #48213 are often sent to get_customer. Second, lookup_order returns dates as Unix timestamps and a numeric status code, while get_customer returns ISO 8601 dates and text statuses; the agent has twice misjudged return deadlines as a result. Third, company policy allows automatic refunds up to $150 and requires a human for larger ones. The prompt states this, yet a few larger refunds have still gone through. Fourth, when the order service times out, lookup_order returns only the word "Error", and the agent either apologizes at once or retries the call endlessly. The team wants each fix to match its cause.

questions.question: Which change best prevents refunds above the $150 limit from going through without a human?
questions.explanation: Policy limits with financial consequences need deterministic enforcement. A pre-execution hook blocks the call and its reason redirects the agent to the escalation tool. More examples are still probabilistic, an email after the fact is detection rather than prevention, and self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated.
options: A pre-execution hook that denies process_refund above $150 and tells the agent to call escalate_to_human
Two further worked examples in the prompt showing the agent escalating a $300 refund instead of processing it
A post-execution hook that emails finance whenever a refund above $150 has been processed by the agent
A step asking the model to state its confidence before each refund and to escalate below 80%

questions.question: Which change is the most robust fix for the misjudged return deadlines?
questions.explanation: The two tools disagree on formats, which can be fixed deterministically after each call. A post-execution hook converts timestamps and status codes before the model reads them. A prompt note depends on the model applying it every time, double-checking doubles the calls, and a bigger model still faces mixed formats.
options: A note in the system prompt explaining that one tool returns Unix timestamps and the other ISO 8601 dates
A post-execution hook that converts dates and status codes into one format before the model reads results
An instruction to double-check every date by calling both tools again for each order that is discussed
A switch to a larger model so that the agent reasons better about dates in several formats

questions.question: What should lookup_order return when the order service times out?
questions.explanation: A timeout is a transient failure, so the result should carry the error flag, a category, a retryable marker and a short description. That lets the agent retry sensibly or explain the delay. The bare word "Error" caused today's behavior, an empty success hides the outage, and ending the session abandons the customer.
options: The single word "Error", plus a note to the agent to apologize to the customer straight away
An empty list marked as successful, so that the conversation can simply continue without a break
A result with the error flag set, a transient category, a retryable marker and a short description
An exception that ends the whole support session so that nothing further can go wrong

questions.question: Which two changes would best stop pasted order numbers from being sent to get_customer? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: Both causes are in the definitions the model reads: one-line descriptions that do not separate the tools, and a keyword-heavy prompt line that ties every order question to the customer lookup. Rewriting the descriptions and the prompt line fixes them. A keyword router overrides the model, merging the tools hides the ambiguity, and temperature does not change what the tools mean.
options: Rewrite both descriptions with accepted identifier formats, example queries and a boundary between the tools
Reword the system-prompt line to say when a customer lookup is needed instead of tying every order question to it
Add a keyword router that overrides the model whenever a message contains the word "order" in any form
Merge all four tools into one tool that handles every kind of request, so there is nothing to choose between
Lower the temperature so that the agent chooses tools more predictably from one conversation to the next

caseStudies.title: Meridian Insights: A Research Assistant That Misses Things
caseStudies.scenario: Meridian Insights, a consulting firm, has built a research assistant with the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to four subagents: web search, document analysis, synthesis and report writing. In a test run on "the economics of battery recycling", the coordinator created three search tasks (collection logistics, recycling costs and recovered-metal prices) and launched them one per turn, so the run took six minutes. It then invoked the synthesis agent with the instruction "combine the findings from the earlier agents". The agent produced a generic overview with no sources, and it kept trying web searches because it had been configured with the same toolset as the search agent. Reviewers also noticed that the report said nothing about regulation or labor, even though each subagent had completed its task. Finally, when the search agent timed out on one task, it returned the message "search unavailable", and the coordinator carried on without noticing that one subtopic had no sources at all.

questions.question: Which change would most reduce the six-minute run time?
questions.explanation: The three searches are independent, so launching them from a single coordinator response lets them run concurrently, and the time approaches that of the slowest one. Merging them into one subagent serializes the work, a smaller model only shortens each step, and a higher turn limit does not change the schedule.
options: Have the coordinator emit all three search launch calls in one response, since the tasks are independent
Merge the three search tasks into one subagent prompt so that only a single launch is needed
Use a smaller model for the coordinator so that each of its turns completes more quickly
Increase the coordinator's maximum number of turns so that it can process more tasks per run

questions.question: Why did the synthesis agent produce a generic overview without sources, and what is the fix?
questions.explanation: Subagents start with an isolated context, so "the findings from the earlier agents" meant nothing to the synthesis agent. The fix is to pass the complete findings in its prompt as structured records that keep source details. Temperature and summary length are unrelated, and letting it search for itself duplicates work and invites out-of-role behavior.
options: Subagent context is isolated, so it never saw the findings; pass them as structured records with sources
Its temperature was too low for synthesis, so raising it would make the writing more specific and detailed
The search agent's summaries were too long to digest, so the search agent should be told to send shorter ones
It lacks the web-search tools it needs, so it should be given them to find the sources on its own

questions.question: How should the synthesis agent's tools be handled?
questions.explanation: The agent searches because search tools are in its toolset. Restricting each subagent to the tools of its role removes the temptation deterministically. A prompt line is probabilistic, more search tools make the problem worse, and a cap of two searches still allows out-of-role behavior.
options: Keep all of its tools and add a prompt line telling it not to search for anything
Add more search tools to its toolset so that each search it performs is more accurate
Restrict it to the tools its role needs, which removes web search from its toolset
Let it keep searching, but cap it at two search calls per run to limit the damage

questions.question: Which two changes address the missing regulation and labor coverage and the unnoticed timeout? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: The coverage gap comes from the coordinator's narrow decomposition, so it should enumerate the dimensions of the topic before delegating. The unnoticed timeout needs structured error context so the coordinator can recover. Writing sections from general knowledge loses sourcing, an empty success suppresses the failure, and a call cap does not target either problem.
options: Have the coordinator list the major dimensions of the topic, including regulation and labor, before delegating, and assign them across subagents
Have subagents return structured error context (failure type, attempted query, partial results) so the coordinator can react to a timeout
Ask the report agent to add sections on regulation and labor from its general knowledge of the subject
Return an empty result marked as successful when a search times out, so that the output format stays uniform
Limit the whole run to three subagent calls so that costs stay predictable from one run to the next

caseStudies.title: Orbit Labs: A Developer Productivity Agent
caseStudies.scenario: Orbit Labs gives its engineers a developer-productivity agent built on the Claude Agent SDK. It uses the built-in Read, Write, Bash, Grep and Glob tools plus three MCP servers: a shared Jira server defined in the repository's .mcp.json, a deploy-calendar server the team wrote for its release rules, and a symbol-aware code-search server that one engineer, Priya, runs privately. The main codebase, ledger-core, has about 2,800 files. Asked "where is the retry logic for payment webhooks?", the agent reads dozens of files before answering and often runs out of context. Priya's search server is described only as "Searches code", and the agent keeps using Grep instead of it. The Jira entry in .mcp.json currently has a personal access token pasted in as plain text. Priya also keeps a named session, webhook-audit, in which she mapped the payment module last week. Since then colleagues have rewritten six of its files, and when she resumed the session yesterday, the agent confidently described functions that no longer exist.

questions.question: What is the best way for the agent to answer the question about the webhook retry logic?
questions.explanation: Building understanding incrementally keeps context focused: search file contents for entry points, then read only the files the results point to. Reading a whole directory wastes context, file-name length says nothing about relevance, and asking the engineer first delays work the agent can start itself.
options: Search for webhook and retry terms to find entry points, then read only the files that matter
Read every file under the payments directory first, in order, so that nothing at all is missed
Use Glob to list all files in the repository and then read the ones with the longest names first
Ask the engineer to point to the right directory before doing anything else in the codebase

questions.question: How should the Jira entry in .mcp.json be changed?
questions.explanation: Environment variable expansion keeps the committed file free of secrets while every engineer supplies the value locally, and the exposed token must be rotated because it is already in history. Moving the file, encoding the token, or ignoring the file each break sharing or leave the secret exposed.
options: Replace the pasted token with ${JIRA_TOKEN}, have each engineer set it, and rotate the exposed token
Move the file into each engineer's home directory so that the token is no longer in the repository
Encode the pasted token in base64 so that it is not readable at a glance to anyone browsing the file
Keep the token as it is but add the file to the ignore list so that it is not committed again

questions.question: The agent keeps using Grep instead of Priya's symbol-aware search server. What is the most effective fix?
questions.explanation: The agent chooses from descriptions, and "Searches code" gives it no reason to prefer the server. Expanding the description with capabilities, outputs and when to prefer the tool addresses the cause. Removing Grep for everyone is heavy-handed, project scope does not change preference, and renaming the tool to match a built-in adds confusion.
options: Expand the server's tool description with what it understands beyond text, what it returns, when to use it
Remove Grep from the agent's tools for every engineer, so that the code-search server is the only choice
Move the server into the committed project file so that it takes priority over the built-in search tools
Rename the tool to Grep so that the agent treats it as though it were the familiar built-in one

questions.question: Which two approaches are sound ways for Priya to continue her webhook-audit work? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: The old session is mostly valid but six files changed, so either resume with a note naming those files, or start fresh from a short summary of what still holds. Relying on the old analysis keeps stale results, forking copies the same stale history, and the agent cannot tell which files changed unless it is told.
options: Resume the session and list the six rewritten files so that the agent re-reads them before answering
Start a new session seeded with a short summary of the findings that are still valid
Resume the session and rely on the earlier analysis because it was thorough and carefully checked
Fork the session so that the copy refreshes its own file contents without being told what changed
Ask the agent to decide for itself which of the files might have changed since the analysis

compare.scenario: A team is deciding how its agent loop should decide when to stop calling the model. Which stop condition is the better choice?
compare.optionA: Stop when the response's stop reason is end_turn, with a turn limit kept only as a handled safety net.
compare.optionB: Stop when the response text contains the word "finished", or after ten iterations, whichever comes first.
compare.why: The stop reason is the structured signal that the model has finished. The combined condition looks cautious because it has two triggers, but phrase matching depends on wording the model may never use, and a bare iteration count either truncates legitimate long tasks or lets short ones end on a coincidence.

compare.scenario: A coordinator must have a synthesis subagent write a cited report from search results gathered by an earlier subagent. Which delegation is better?
compare.optionA: Pass the complete findings in the prompt as structured records, each with claim, excerpt, source and date.
compare.optionB: Tell the synthesis agent to combine the results the search agent produced earlier and to cite them.
compare.why: A subagent has an isolated context, so only what is in its prompt exists for it. The short instruction is tempting because the search agent really did produce the results, but the synthesis agent cannot see them, so it will invent or generalize, and prose would lose the attribution anyway.

compare.scenario: A coordinator must research five independent regional markets. Which launch strategy is better?
compare.optionA: Emit five subagent launch calls in one response so the markets are researched concurrently.
compare.optionB: Launch one subagent per turn so that each result can shape the next prompt.
compare.why: The markets do not depend on each other, so running them together cuts the time to roughly the slowest single task. Sequential launching is tempting because earlier results could refine later prompts, but that benefit is imaginary when the tasks are independent and the cost is the sum of all durations.

compare.scenario: An agent must never issue a refund to a customer who has not been verified. Which control is better?
compare.optionA: A gate in code that rejects refund calls until the customer lookup has returned a verified id.
compare.optionB: A system-prompt section that explains the verification rule and gives three worked examples.
compare.why: The rule has financial consequences, so it needs a deterministic guarantee. Worked examples are tempting because they are cheap and do improve compliance, but any prompt-based approach leaves a non-zero chance that a refund goes out unverified.

compare.scenario: A long session mapped a large codebase. Since then sixty commits have changed most of the modules it examined. Which way of continuing is better?
compare.optionA: Start a new session seeded with a structured summary of the findings that still hold.
compare.optionB: Resume the old session and ask the agent to be careful about anything that might have changed.
compare.why: Most of the old tool results are now wrong, and a fresh start avoids carrying them forward. Resuming is tempting because it keeps every detail, but the agent cannot re-observe files by being told to be careful, so stale content keeps influencing its answers.

compare.scenario: One process_document tool takes a mode parameter, and its modes return completely different outputs: a list of fields, a prose summary, and a verification verdict. The agent often chooses the wrong mode. Which design is better?
compare.optionA: Split it into extract_fields, summarize_document and verify_claim tools, each with its own contract.
compare.optionB: Keep one tool and describe the output shape of each mode at length in its description.
compare.why: Distinct purposes with distinct output contracts give the model clear choices and callers predictable results. Keeping one tool with longer documentation is tempting because it means fewer tools, but the model must still pick a mode correctly and parse three shapes from the same name.

compare.scenario: A refund tool must report that a request falls outside the 90-day window. Which response is better?
compare.optionA: A result flagged as an error, categorized as a business error, marked not retryable, with a customer-friendly explanation.
compare.optionB: A result flagged as an error with the text "Request failed", so the agent can try again with different arguments.
compare.why: The agent needs to know the failure is final and what to tell the customer. The generic version uses the error flag, which makes it tempting, but a vague message invites retries that can never succeed and gives the agent nothing to say.

compare.scenario: A team wants every developer to have the same Postgres MCP server, with the connection credentials kept out of the repository. Which setup is better?
compare.optionA: A project .mcp.json that references the connection string as ${DATABASE_URL}, supplied from each developer's environment.
compare.optionB: Each developer adds the server to their own user config with the connection string typed in.
compare.why: The shared file gives everyone the same, version-controlled setup while the secret stays local. Per-developer user configs also avoid committing the secret, which makes them tempting, but every developer must configure the server by hand and the setups drift apart.

compare.scenario: A pipeline must run extract_metadata before anything else and then let the model choose follow-up tools from the result. Which approach is better?
compare.optionA: Force extract_metadata on the first request, then continue on automatic tool choice.
compare.optionB: Instruct the model in the system prompt to call extract_metadata first on every task.
compare.why: Forcing the named tool guarantees the opening step, and automatic choice afterwards leaves the model free to pick enrichment tools. The prompt instruction is simpler and usually works, which makes it tempting, but it cannot guarantee the step happens.
